lesson.title: The best for whom?
lesson.subtitle: The total, the worst-off, and a fair rule agreed with people

video.title: The best for whom?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — education lecturer (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Scores, and first come, first served
Three ways to judge a plan

scenes.visual: Dr Farah in a staff room; five teachers queue in front of a board with five classes on it.
scenes.animation: Classes on the board are taken one by one; the last teacher looks at the only one left.
scenes.narration: Five teachers, five classes, and a head teacher who says: the most senior choose first. It sounds fair, and it’s quick. But what happens to the teacher who chooses last?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: the best plan, and who it’s best for.

scenes.visual: A five-by-five table of scores; Amina’s row is mostly high, Karim’s row has one 9 and low numbers.
scenes.animation: Rows light up as each teacher is named.
scenes.narration: Each teacher has a score for each class, from zero to nine: how well they suit it. Amina is good at almost everything, and loves maths. Karim is really good only at maths. Each class needs one teacher, and each teacher takes one class.

scenes.visual: Arrows show each teacher picking in turn; Karim’s card shows a 2 in red.
scenes.animation: Picks happen one after another; the total counts up to 29.
scenes.narration: Amina chooses first and takes maths, her favourite. The others choose in turn, each taking their best class still free. Karim is left with science, a two out of nine. The total is twenty-nine.

scenes.visual: Two columns: first come (29, lowest 2) against the best total (39, lowest 6).
scenes.animation: The right column fills pair by pair; its totals glow.
scenes.narration: Now give maths to Karim, science to Leila, English to Yusuf, art to Zainab and history to Amina. The total is thirty-nine, the best there is. And the lowest score is six, not two.

scenes.visual: Three measuring tools: a sum sign, a person at the bottom of a ladder, a gap between two bars.
scenes.animation: Each measure appears as it is named.
scenes.on_screen_text: Three ways to judge a plan
scenes.narration: So how do you judge a plan? Look at the total: how good it is overall. Look at the worst-off: the lowest score anyone gets. And look at the gap between the best and the worst. A plan can win on one and lose on another.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds the first-come table. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Under first come, first served, who comes off worst?

scenes.visual: Karim with a science book upside down; then Amina handing the maths book to Karim.
scenes.animation: Check badge on ‘Karim’; Amina’s score slides from 9 to 6.
scenes.narration: Karim, with a class he can hardly teach, and his pupils lose too. But the better plan asks Amina to give up her favourite: she drops from nine to six. That’s a real cost to her, so ask it openly, and fairly, don’t just order it.

scenes.visual: Three rule cards side by side, each with a small plus and minus.
scenes.animation: Cards appear as each rule is said.
scenes.narration: Several rules sound fair. First come, first served is quick, but an early choice can take someone’s only good option. The best total is good for the school, but someone may give up a favourite. Looking after the worst-off makes the lowest score as high as it can be.

scenes.visual: A staff meeting: the scores on a flip chart, teachers nodding, one raising a hand to correct a number.
scenes.animation: A score is crossed out and corrected; heads nod.
scenes.narration: Whatever rule you use, agree it with the people affected before anyone knows who wins. Say the rule out loud and show the numbers. Let people correct a score that’s wrong. People accept a plan they can understand.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: the score table, two buttons, totals 29 and 39.
scenes.animation: The table fills with picks; then zeros and lines appear step by step.
scenes.narration: In the app, press Let them choose in turn, and see first come, first served. Then press Run and watch the Hungarian method find the best total. Change Karim’s maths score, and run both again.

scenes.visual: Amina with a duty rota: one pupil’s name next to ‘clean the toilets’ every week. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. For class duties, the plan with the best total gives one pupil the job nobody wants, every single week. Is that fair?

scenes.visual: Summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Not necessarily: a great total can still leave one person with the worst job every week. Remember: judge a plan by its total, its worst-off and its gap. First come, first served can waste good matches. And agree the rule with the people it affects.

scenes.visual: Amina’s class with a duty chart; pupils vote with raised hands.
scenes.animation: Names move around the duty chart; hands go up.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: plan class duties fairly. Pupils score each job from one to five. Compare first come, first served with a plan that lifts the lowest score, and rotate the hardest job. Then ask the class which plan they’d choose, and why.

checkpoints.prompt: Under first come, first served, who comes off worst?

options.text: Karim, with a class he can hardly teach

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — Karim gets science, a 2 out of 9, because Amina took the only class he is good at. His pupils lose too.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — look for the lowest score: Karim gets science, 2 out of 9, because the maths class he’s good at was taken first.

checkpoints.prompt: The plan with the best total gives one pupil the job nobody wants, every week. Is it fair?

options.text: Yes: the total is the best, so it’s fair
Not necessarily: check the worst-off, and share the hard job
Only if that pupil agreed once

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a high total can hide one person who always loses. Check the worst-off, and rotate or share the hard job.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the total doesn’t show who carries the worst job every week. Check the worst-off too, and share the hard job.
